summary: This informational document describes the bitstream format and decoding process of Advanced Professional Video (APV), a codec for visually lossless compression aimed at recording and post-production. It is an informational description of the format.

eli5.summary: APV is a way to shrink video files for professionals without making them look worse.

questions: what color formats does apv support
subtitle: A professional video compression format for recording and editing without visible quality loss.

tldr.problem: Professional video recording and post-production require high quality, high throughput, and the ability to re-encode multiple times without degradation, but existing codecs either lose quality or are too slow.
tldr.mechanism: APV (Advanced Professional Video) is an intra-frame-only codec that compresses each frame independently using transform coding and entropy coding, supporting visually lossless quality, high bit rates (up to a few Gbps), and tile-based parallel processing.
tldr.outcome: APV provides visually lossless compression suitable for 2K, 4K, and 8K professional video workflows, with support for multiple color formats and metadata including HDR10/HDR10+.

facts.label: Bit depths
facts.value: 10 to 16 bits per sample (10, 12 bits currently profiled)

today: RFC 9924 is an Informational RFC documenting APV as a professional video codec. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the current specification for APV implementations.

sections.title: APV: Visually Lossless Video Compression
sections.content:
APV (Advanced Professional Video) is a professional video codec designed for recording and post-production workflows. Unlike general-purpose codecs that must balance quality, speed, and file size, APV prioritizes visual quality and throughput. It uses intra-frame coding—each frame is encoded independently, without prediction from previous or future frames—which allows low-latency encoding, fast seeking within a file, and the ability to re-encode without drift or quality cascading.

APV is visually lossless, meaning the compressed image is perceptually identical to the original even under close inspection. This is critical for professionals: an editor working on a color grade, a visual effects shot, or mastering needs to know the compressed version is faithful to the source. APV achieves this while supporting high bit rates (up to a few Gbps) for 2K, 4K, and 8K content, and it includes features like frame tiling for parallel encoding and decoding, and metadata for HDR10 and HDR10+.
sections.eli5: APV is a video squeeze that makes files smaller while keeping them looking perfect. Professionals use it because they can edit the video many times and it never gets worse, and they can work on huge 4K and 8K videos without waiting for encoding.

sections.title: Codec Design: Intra-Frame, Transform, and Entropy Coding
sections.content:
APV encodes each frame as a collection of macroblocks (16x16 pixel blocks for luma, with chroma at half resolution). Each macroblock is partitioned into smaller blocks, which are transformed using a discrete cosine transform (DCT), quantized, and then entropy coded. The low complexity of intra-frame-only coding—no need to search for motion or maintain frame buffers—means encoding and decoding can happen quickly, with minimal latency.

The codec supports multiple chroma sampling formats: 4:0:0 (monochrome), 4:2:2 (half-width chroma), 4:4:4 (full resolution chroma), and 4:4:4:4 (full resolution with alpha). Bit depths range from 10 to 16 bits per sample, preserving the precision of professional capture. The tile structure allows a frame to be divided into rectangular tiles that are independently encoded, enabling parallel processing on multi-core systems and allowing software decoders to process regions of interest independently.
sections.eli5: APV breaks each video frame into small blocks, transforms them mathematically to find redundancy, then squeezes out the redundancy with smart coding. It can split frames into tiles so many cores can work on them at once.

sections.title: Color, Metadata, and Profiles
sections.content:
APV handles multiple color representations: luma and chroma (YCbCr or YCgCo), RGB, and other tri-stimulus formats like XYZ. This flexibility supports both video and image pipelines. The codec carries rich metadata about color space, gamma curves, mastering display color volume (for HDR10), and content light levels. It also supports user-defined metadata, allowing workflows to embed custom information like annotation data or timing information.

The RFC defines eight profiles: 422-10, 422-12, 444-10, 444-12, 4444-10, 4444-12, 400-10, corresponding to different chroma formats and bit depths. Each profile has levels and bands that constrain maximum resolution, frame rate, and bit rate, allowing decoders to declare their capabilities and enabling interoperability. The bitstream is self-describing: a frame header contains color information, quantization parameters, and tile structure.
sections.eli5: APV knows about colors from different sources—video, images, cinema—and can carry information about how bright things should be (HDR) and what the professional monitor should show. Different profiles let devices declare which sizes and speeds they can handle.

sections.title: Bitstream Structure and Access Units
sections.content:
An APV bitstream consists of Access Units (AUs), each containing a signature ('aPv1'), followed by one or more Primitive Bitstream Units (PBUs). A PBU is tagged with a type (primary frame, non-primary frame, metadata, filler, or access unit info) and a group ID for associating frames with metadata. A primary frame is the main image; non-primary frames might be additional views, depth maps, or alpha channels. Each PBU has a size field, allowing decoders to skip over data they do not understand.

Within a frame, tile size fields precede each tile's data, enabling a decoder to identify tile boundaries without parsing tile headers. This structure supports streaming: a decoder can begin playback after receiving a complete access unit, and parallel decoders can process tiles independently. The bitstream is specified in C pseudocode using big-endian byte order, with detailed decoding processes for quantization scaling, inverse transformation, and sample reconstruction.
sections.eli5: An APV file is a sequence of frames, each wrapped in a container with a signature and metadata tags. Inside each frame are tiles that can be decoded in parallel. This design lets streaming players start playing before the whole file is available.

sections.title: Status and Implementations
sections.content:
RFC 9924 is an Informational RFC documenting APV as a professional video format. It does not represent an IETF consensus and is not on the standards track. The specification is a complete description of the bitstream format and decoding process, enabling independent implementations. Reference implementations exist in open-source projects including OpenAPV, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), and FFmpeg, making the codec accessible to a broad range of applications.

APV is designed for professional workflows where visual quality is paramount and file re-encoding is common. Unlike streaming codecs that optimize for low latency or low bitrate, APV emphasizes fidelity and re-encodeability, making it suitable for archival, post-production, and professional content distribution where the cost of encoding is a one-time investment, and the value of quality is measured over years of reuse.
sections.eli5: APV is documented so anyone can build tools that read and write it. Video software companies use it for editing, and archive projects use it because they know the quality will not degrade over decades of reuse.
